title: Cramer's Rule
body:
**Cramer's Rule** solves a [[System of Linear Equations]] $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ with $A$
square and invertible, by writing each unknown as a ratio of [[Determinant|determinants]]:

$$
x_i = \frac{\det A_i}{\det A}
$$

where $A_i$ is $A$ with its $i$th column replaced by $\mathbf{b}$.

Example, for $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 11
\end{bmatrix}$: $\det A = 1$, $\det A_1 = \det\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 11 & 3\end{bmatrix} = 1$,
$\det A_2 = \det\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 11\end{bmatrix} = 2$, so $x = 1, y = 2$.

Two things to take from it:

- **It is a theoretical result, not an algorithm.** It needs $n+1$ determinants, so it is
  $O(n!)$ by cofactor expansion or $O(n^4)$ if each determinant is row-reduced. Plain
  [[Gaussian Elimination]] is $O(n^3)$ and gives every unknown at once. Same "the closed form is
  the slow way" lesson as the adjoint formula in [[Matrix Inverse]].
- **It is useful when you want one unknown out of many**, or when you need $x_i$ as an explicit
  algebraic expression in the entries rather than as a number.

It requires $\det A \neq 0$, so it only applies in the one-solution case and says nothing about
inconsistent or underdetermined systems.
